Looking at this problem, I need to find how many indices $n$ have $a_n = 111$.

## Setting Up the Binary-Operation Correspondence

**Key observation:** Write $n$ in binary as $1\,b_1\,b_2\,\dots\,b_k$ (leading 1). Then $a_n$ is obtained from the starting value $1$ by applying, for each bit $b_i$ (left to right):
- $b_i = 0$: the operation $v \mapsto v + 1$ (corresponding to $a_{2m} = a_m + 1$),
- $b_i = 1$: the operation $v \mapsto 10v$ (corresponding to $a_{2m+1} = 10\,a_m$).

**Proof by induction on the number of bits:** The base case is $n=1$ (binary "1"), giving $a_1 = 1$. If $n = 2m$ (binary of $m$ followed by 0), then $a_n = a_m + 1$, matching the "+1" operation. If $n = 2m+1$ (binary of $m$ followed by 1), then $a_n = 10\,a_m$, matching the "×10" operation. ∎

**Example check:** $n = 13 = 1101_2$. Operations: ×10, +1, ×10. Value: $1 \xrightarrow{\times 10} 10 \xrightarrow{+1} 11 \xrightarrow{\times 10} 110$. Indeed $a_{13} = 10\,a_6 = 10 \cdot 11 = 110$. ✓

## Counting Paths via Reverse Recursion

The question becomes: **how many sequences of operations** (each being $+1$ or $\times 10$), applied to $1$, produce $111$?

Define $f(v)$ = number of ways to reach $1$ from $v$ by reversing operations:
- Reverse of $+1$: $v \to v-1$ (valid for $v \geq 2$),
- Reverse of $\times 10$: $v \to v/10$ (valid when $10 \mid v$).

**Recursion:**
$$f(1) = 1, \qquad f(v) = f(v-1) + \begin{cases} f(v/10) & \text{if } 10 \mid v \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \quad (v \geq 2).$$

Each distinct path corresponds to a distinct operation sequence, hence a distinct binary string, hence a distinct index $n$. So the answer is $f(111)$.

## Computing $f(111)$

Between consecutive multiples of 10, $f$ is constant (since only $-1$ steps apply). At each multiple $10k$, $f$ jumps by $f(k)$.

|-------|-------------|

| $f(2)$–$f(9)$ | $1$ |
| $f(10) = f(9)+f(1) = 1+1$ | $2$ |
| $f(11)$–$f(19)$ | $2$ |
| $f(20) = f(19)+f(2) = 2+1$ | $3$ |

| $f(81)$–$f(89)$ | $9$ |
| $f(90) = f(89)+f(9) = 9+1$ | $10$ |
| $f(91)$–$f(99)$ | $10$ |
| $f(100) = f(99)+f(10) = 10+2$ | $12$ |
| $f(101)$–$f(109)$ | $12$ |
| $f(110) = f(109)+f(11) = 12+2$ | $14$ |
| $f(111) = f(110)$ (since $10 \nmid 111$) | $\mathbf{14}$ |

## Verification of a Sample Path

One path: $111 \xleftarrow{-1} 110 \xleftarrow{\div 10} 11 \xleftarrow{-1} 10 \xleftarrow{\div 10} 1$.
Forward: $1 \xrightarrow{\times 10} 10 \xrightarrow{+1} 11 \xrightarrow{\times 10} 110 \xrightarrow{+1} 111$.
Binary: $11010_2 = 26$. Check: $a_{26} = a_{13}+1 = 110+1 = 111$. ✓

Another path: $111 \xleftarrow{-1} 110 \xleftarrow{-1} \cdots \xleftarrow{-1} 100 \xleftarrow{\div 10} 10 \xleftarrow{\div 10} 1$.
Forward: $1 \xrightarrow{\times 10} 10 \xrightarrow{\times 10} 100 \xrightarrow{+1 \times 11} 111$.
Binary: $1110000000000_2$. This gives a valid distinct index. ✓

Every path produces a distinct binary string (distinct operation sequence), so all 14 paths yield 14 distinct indices $n$ with $a_n = 111$.

## Answer

The number 111 appears in the sequence $\boxed{14}$ times.
